subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Complex multigenic disorders arise from the combined effect of many genetic variants and environmental factors. They underlie common diseases such as type 2 diabetes and hypertension, requiring a nuanced clinical approach.

sections.p: These disorders are not caused by a single gene mutation but by the additive or interactive effects of numerous variants, each contributing modest risk, together with lifestyle and exposures.
b: Most common adult diseases are polygenic
Risk is quantified by polygenic risk scores in research

sections.p: Each variant may alter protein function, expression, or regulation. When many such changes accumulate, pathways like insulin signaling or vascular tone become dysregulated.
b: Epigenetic changes can amplify genetic risk

sections.p: Regulatory networks (transcription factors, microRNAs) integrate signals from multiple genes. Disruption of these networks can shift homeostasis toward disease.
b: Common variants often lie in non‑coding regulatory regions
Network analysis helps identify key nodes for therapy

sections.p: When the cumulative genetic load exceeds a threshold, physiological systems fail. For example, impaired β‑cell function plus insulin resistance leads to type 2 diabetes.
b: Multiple small‑effect alleles → large clinical effect
Environmental triggers (obesity, diet, infection) tip the balance

sections.p: Understanding polygenic risk guides screening, prevention, and personalized therapy. It also explains why family history is important even without a single Mendelian mutation.
b: Risk stratification informs earlier lifestyle intervention
Pharmacogenomics may modify drug choice (e.g., antihypertensives)

t.b: Does the patient have a high genetic predisposition? A high PRS suggests intensified monitoring and preventive measures.
Is glucose control impaired? Elevated HbA1c confirms diabetes, prompting treatment regardless of genetic risk.
Is hypertension present? Persistent elevation confirms disease; genetics informs risk but not diagnosis.

sections.p: Focus on the concept of multiple low‑penetrance genes plus environment, examples of common polygenic diseases, and how they differ from Mendelian disorders.
b: Role of lifestyle in modifying genetic risk

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden cardiovascular collapse in a high‑risk patient

faq.q: How is a polygenic disease diagnosed?
faq.a: Through clinical criteria (e.g., blood glucose, blood pressure) plus family/history; genetic testing is research‑focused, not routine.

faq.q: Can lifestyle change overcome genetic risk?
faq.a: Yes, healthy diet, exercise, and weight control can markedly lower disease incidence even in high‑risk individuals.

faq.q: Are polygenic risk scores used in everyday practice?
faq.a: Currently they are mainly research tools; some centres use them for risk stratification in specific populations.

exam: Explain why type 2 diabetes is considered a complex multigenic disorder.
List two ways environment interacts with genetic risk in hypertension.
Differentiate polygenic inheritance from Mendelian inheritance in terms of family patterns.
